blocks.text:
Design the system behind a news aggregator, the kind of product that pulls articles from thousands of external publishers and presents readers with a single, unified feed. The hard problem here is not fetching content, it is recognizing that when a major event happens, fifty different publishers all cover it within the hour, and a good aggregator has to recognize all fifty of those articles as the same underlying story and present them as one clustered item with multiple sources, not as fifty separate, redundant entries flooding the feed.

The technique that makes this tractable at scale is treating near-duplicate detection as an approximate, similarity-based clustering problem rather than an exact one, using a combination called MinHash and Locality Sensitive Hashing to avoid ever comparing a new article against the entire accumulated history of everything ever ingested.
blocks.content:
Design the system behind a news aggregator, the kind of product that pulls articles from thousands of external publishers and presents readers with a single, unified feed. The hard problem here is not fetching content, it is recognizing that when a major event happens, fifty different publishers all cover it within the hour, and a good aggregator has to recognize all fifty of those articles as the same underlying story and present them as one clustered item with multiple sources, not as fifty separate, redundant entries flooding the feed.

The technique that makes this tractable at scale is treating near-duplicate detection as an approximate, similarity-based clustering problem rather than an exact one, using a combination called MinHash and Locality Sensitive Hashing to avoid ever comparing a new article against the entire accumulated history of everything ever ingested.

blocks.text: The system should continuously ingest articles from a large number of external sources, each on its own publishing schedule. It should detect when multiple articles from different sources are covering the same real-world event and group them into a single story. It should present a ranked feed of current stories, each showing a representative article plus a count or list of the other sources also covering it. Rankings should reflect a story's importance, weighing how many independent sources are covering it and how recent it is.

Rankings should reflect a story's importance, weighing how many independent sources are covering it and how recent it is.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter most, and the first shapes the entire architecture.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter most, and the first shapes the entire architecture.

blocks.alt: Scalable deduplication, source isolation, freshness for breaking news, accurate clustering, and availability

blocks.text: Deduplication has to scale as the corpus of ingested articles grows without bound, comparing every new article against everything ever seen is simply not viable at any meaningful volume. Source isolation matters because one flaky or slow external source should never be able to delay or degrade ingestion from every other source. Freshness matters because the whole value of a news aggregator collapses if a genuinely breaking story takes hours to surface. Clustering accuracy is a real balancing act, merging two genuinely different stories together is just as much a failure as failing to merge two articles about the same event. And the feed needs to stay available even while ingestion for a subset of sources is degraded or temporarily down.

blocks.text: This design assumes a tunable similarity threshold decides what counts as the same story, accepting that both false merges and false splits are possible at the margins, and that threshold is a genuine product decision rather than a purely technical one. Most sources are assumed to support only polling, such as RSS, rather than push-based delivery, so ingestion is built around a scheduler rather than assuming sources will notify the system proactively. Personalization is out of scope for this version, noted as a future layer. Articles are treated as immutable once ingested, a later correction from the source is treated as a new version rather than mutating history in place.

blocks.text: Say the platform polls tens of thousands of external sources continuously, ingesting a few million new articles a day in total. Comparing every new article against every previously ingested article, even at a modest ingestion rate, would mean billions of pairwise comparisons a day, an amount of work that grows quadratically and quickly becomes impossible. MinHash and Locality Sensitive Hashing instead let each new article be compared only against the handful of other articles that happen to land in the same hash buckets, turning a problem that scales with the square of total corpus size into one that scales with the size of a small candidate set per article.

blocks.text: A pool of poller workers fetches from each configured source on that source's own schedule, isolating any one source's slowness or failures from every other source's ingestion. Fetched articles flow through an ingest queue into normalizer workers, which extract a common schema, title, body, publish time, from whatever format each source originally used. Normalized articles then reach the deduplication engine, which computes a compact similarity signature for each one and checks it against existing clusters before deciding whether it joins an existing story or starts a new one. Stories are ranked continuously and served to readers from a cache that refreshes on a short interval.

blocks.alt: Sources are polled on their own schedules into an ingest queue, normalized, then deduplicated using MinHash and LSH into stories, which are ranked and served through a cached feed

blocks.text: An article's text is broken into overlapping word shingles, short sequences of consecutive words, and several MinHash signatures are computed from that shingle set, each one a compact number that approximates how similar two documents' shingle sets are without needing to compare every shingle directly. Locality Sensitive Hashing then groups articles into a small number of buckets such that articles with similar signatures are very likely to land in the same bucket together, which is exactly what lets a new article be checked against only the small handful of other articles already sharing its buckets, rather than the entire corpus.

A feed request is served from a recently cached ranking whenever available, recomputed only once that cache has expired

blocks.text: The happy path is exactly the ingestion flow above, a new article checked against a small candidate set and either joining an existing story or starting a new one. The workflow worth walking through separately is a genuinely major breaking event, where dozens of sources publish within minutes of each other. The very first article on the event creates a brand new story with no existing candidates to match against. Each subsequent article from a different source computes its own signature, lands in largely overlapping LSH buckets with that first article, and joins the same story, causing that story's sourceCount to climb rapidly, which is exactly the signal the ranking service uses to push a genuinely major story toward the top of the feed.

blocks.alt: Polled articles flow through an ingest queue to normalizer workers, then through a deduplication queue to the workers that actually cluster them into stories

blocks.text: Splitting ingestion, normalization, and deduplication into separate queued stages means a slowdown in deduplication, the most computationally interesting stage, never blocks the poller workers from continuing to fetch fresh content from every other source.

blocks.alt: Every configured source is partitioned evenly across poller workers, so a single worker is never responsible for an unreasonable share of total sources

blocks.text: Partitioning by source, rather than round-robin across arbitrary requests, keeps the isolation property from section 7.2 intact, one worker's assigned sources having trouble does not spill over into another worker's entirely separate set.

blocks.alt: Growing ingest or deduplication queue depth triggers adding more normalizer or deduplication workers

blocks.text: Because LSH bucketing keeps each article's candidate comparison set small and roughly constant regardless of total corpus size, the deduplication engine scales by adding workers in proportion to ingestion volume, not in proportion to how much history has already accumulated.

blocks.text: Articles and stories are partitioned by ingestion time, since recent content dominates both read and dedup-candidate traffic overwhelmingly, and older stories can be moved to cheaper, colder storage once they are no longer realistically going to receive new matching articles.

blocks.text: A brand-new article can, for a short window, appear as its own separate story before a slightly delayed deduplication pass merges it into the correct existing one, which is a perfectly acceptable trade given how much simpler and faster this makes the ingestion path compared to demanding instantaneous, perfectly consistent clustering on every single article.

blocks.text: This per-source isolation is a deliberate design choice rather than an incidental property, a shared polling loop across every source would let one badly behaved external endpoint degrade ingestion for the entire platform, exactly the failure mode this architecture is built to avoid.

blocks.alt: Content pulled from an external, untrusted source is sanitized and validated before being stored or ever rendered to a reader; anything suspicious is rejected outright

blocks.text: This is a security concern genuinely specific to aggregating third-party content rather than internally-generated data: an external source, whether compromised or simply malicious, could attempt to inject harmful markup or scripts into what looks like an ordinary article, which is exactly why sanitization happens immediately after ingestion, before that content is ever trusted enough to store or display.

from typing import Dict, List, Set


# Breaks text into overlapping word shingles, the basic unit MinHash
# similarity is computed over.
class Shingler:
    @staticmethod
    def shingle(text: str, shingle_size: int) -> Set[str]:
        words = text.lower().split()
        shingles: Set[str] = set()
        for i in range(0, len(words) - shingle_size + 1):
            shingles.add(" ".join(words[i:i + shingle_size]))
        return shingles


def _string_hash(s: str) -> int:
    # A 32-bit polynomial string hash (same recurrence used by Java's own
    # String.hashCode): deterministic across languages given the same input,
    # which is what keeps the MinHash signatures below comparable.
    h = 0
    for ch in s:
        h = (31 * h + ord(ch)) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    if h >= (1 << 31):
        h -= (1 << 32)
    return h


class _SeededRandom:
    # A small, fixed linear-congruential generator (not Python's own random
    # module) purely so the demo's hash seeds are reproducible byte-for-byte
    # from one run to the next.
    def __init__(self, seed: int):
        self._state = (seed ^ 0x5DEECE66D) & ((1 << 48) - 1)

    def next_int(self) -> int:
        self._state = (self._state * 0x5DEECE66D + 0xB) & ((1 << 48) - 1)
        value = self._state >> 16
        if value >= (1 << 31):
            value -= (1 << 32)
        return value


# Computes a compact MinHash signature for a set of shingles, approximating
# Jaccard similarity between two documents without comparing every shingle.
class MinHasher:
    def __init__(self, num_hashes: int, seed: int):
        rng = _SeededRandom(seed)   # fixed seed, so results are reproducible every run
        self._seeds_a = [rng.next_int() for _ in range(num_hashes)]
        self._seeds_b = [rng.next_int() for _ in range(num_hashes)]

    # For each of several independent hash functions, keeps only the
    # minimum hash value seen across every shingle, producing one compact
    # signature that approximates the document's full shingle set.
    def compute_signature(self, shingles: Set[str]) -> List[int]:
        signature = [None] * len(self._seeds_a)
        for shingle in shingles:
            base_hash = _string_hash(shingle)
            for i in range(len(self._seeds_a)):
                hashed = (self._seeds_a[i] * base_hash + self._seeds_b[i]) & 0x7fffffff
                signature[i] = hashed if signature[i] is None else min(signature[i], hashed)
        return signature


# Groups articles into buckets by bands of their MinHash signature, so a
# new article only needs comparing against whatever few other articles
# already share at least one of its bands.
class LshIndex:
    def __init__(self, band_size: int):
        self._band_size = band_size
        self._bucket_to_article_ids: Dict[str, List[str]] = {}

    def index(self, article_id: str, signature: List[int]) -> None:
        for bucket_key in self._bucket_keys_for(signature):
            self._bucket_to_article_ids.setdefault(bucket_key, []).append(article_id)

    # Returns every other article sharing at least one band with this
    # signature, a small candidate set rather than the entire corpus.
    def find_candidates(self, signature: List[int]) -> Set[str]:
        candidates: Set[str] = set()
        for bucket_key in self._bucket_keys_for(signature):
            candidates.update(self._bucket_to_article_ids.get(bucket_key, []))
        return candidates

    def _bucket_keys_for(self, signature: List[int]) -> List[str]:
        keys = []
        for i in range(0, len(signature), self._band_size):
            end = min(i + self._band_size, len(signature))
            keys.append(f"{i}-{signature[i:end]}")
        return keys


def _format_set(items: Set[str]) -> str:
    return "[" + ", ".join(items) + "]"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Two different outlets covering the exact same product launch, lightly reworded.
    article_a = ("Apple unveiled its new iPhone today at a special event in Cupertino "
                 "featuring an improved camera and longer battery life")
    article_b = ("Apple unveiled its new iPhone today at a special event in Cupertino "
                 "with an improved camera and longer battery life")
    # A genuinely unrelated story.
    article_c = ("Scientists announced a breakthrough in fusion energy research that "
                 "could pave the way for cleaner power generation")

    shingle_size = 3
    num_hashes = 20
    band_size = 4
    seed = 42

    min_hasher = MinHasher(num_hashes, seed)
    lsh_index = LshIndex(band_size)

    shingles_a = Shingler.shingle(article_a, shingle_size)
    shingles_b = Shingler.shingle(article_b, shingle_size)
    shingles_c = Shingler.shingle(article_c, shingle_size)

    signature_a = min_hasher.compute_signature(shingles_a)
    signature_b = min_hasher.compute_signature(shingles_b)
    signature_c = min_hasher.compute_signature(shingles_c)

    lsh_index.index("article-A", signature_a)

    candidates_for_b = lsh_index.find_candidates(signature_b)
    print(f"Candidates found for article B (near duplicate of A): {_format_set(candidates_for_b)}")
    print(f"Article B correctly flags article A as a likely duplicate: {str('article-A' in candidates_for_b).lower()}")

    candidates_for_c = lsh_index.find_candidates(signature_c)
    print(f"Candidates found for article C (unrelated story): {_format_set(candidates_for_c)}")
    print(f"Article C correctly finds no relation to article A: {str(len(candidates_for_c) == 0).lower()}")

    intersection = shingles_a & shingles_b
    union = shingles_a | shingles_b
    true_jaccard = len(intersection) / len(union)
    print(f"True Jaccard similarity between A and B: {true_jaccard}")

items: Architecture: isolated per-source polling feeding a queued pipeline through normalization and MinHash-and-LSH-based deduplication into a story store, ranked and cached for reads.

Capacity: tens of thousands of sources, a few million articles ingested daily, and the stark gap between billions of daily comparisons under a naive approach versus a small, bounded candidate set per article under LSH.
The core technique: MinHash signatures and Locality Sensitive Hashing, worked through with a real, genuinely functional implementation.
Database: individual articles as the source of truth, with a derived Story aggregate carrying a denormalized source count for fast ranking.
End-to-end workflows: ingestion-and-deduplication and feed reads, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: eventual clustering consistency, a brief window as an unmerged duplicate is an accepted trade for ingestion speed.
Trade-offs: exact all-pairs comparison versus MinHash and LSH versus naive exact-text matching, compared directly on comparison cost, accuracy, and where each breaks down.
